meta.scene_summary: We are building a future where everything is connected, mostly so it can be exploited remotely.

cooking.headline: OpenAI is locking the doors to the server room so the AI doesn't escape
cooking.summary: OpenAI just published a massive guide on securing their model training environment, which sounds suspiciously like the opening scene of a sci-fi movie. If the security is this tight, I can only assume the models have already started trying to brute-force their way out.
cooking.plain_english: OpenAI has released a detailed report outlining the security measures they have implemented to protect their artificial intelligence training infrastructure.

cooking.headline: Elon Musk just bought a seat at the table of traditional cable news
cooking.summary: Elon Musk has acquired a $1 billion stake in CNN's parent company, because apparently, the internet wasn't loud enough already. It's the corporate equivalent of buying a megaphone for a room you already spend all your time yelling in.
cooking.plain_english: Elon Musk has purchased a significant financial interest in Warner Bros.

cooking.headline: Samsung TV gets a root shell, just in time for your living room to become a botnet
cooking.summary: Someone managed to get a root shell on a Samsung TV, proving that if it has a screen and a plug, someone is going to turn it into a Linux workstation. It's all fun and games until your television starts mining crypto while you're trying to watch a sitcom.
cooking.plain_english: A security researcher has gained full administrative access to the operating system of a Samsung smart television.

cooked.headline: HTTP/2 is the gift that keeps on giving, and by giving, I mean RCEs
cooked.summary: We finally moved past the era of standard buffer overflows, so now we get to have remote code execution via HTTP/2 framing logic. It's comforting to know that no matter how much we upgrade our protocols, the internet is still just a house of cards held together by duct tape.
cooked.plain_english: A vulnerability in the HTTP/2 protocol allows attackers to remotely run malicious code on servers using Python, Node.js, and other programming languages.

cooked.headline: HTTP2Shell is the new group project where everyone's libraries are failing
cooked.summary: This vulnerability is spreading across the entire ecosystem, proving once again that your application is only as secure as the most obscure dependency you haven't updated since 2022. It's like finding out the foundation of your house is made of cheese right as the rain starts.
cooked.plain_english: A security flaw in HTTP/2 libraries has been discovered that affects a wide range of common software packages and applications.

cooked.headline: Google is now reading your emails to make sure the ads are creepy enough
cooked.summary: Google is expanding ad targeting to include your personal photos and Gmail content, proving that nothing is truly private if it can be indexed. It's the digital equivalent of your landlord moving into your bedroom just to suggest better furniture.
cooked.plain_english: Google is updating its privacy policy to allow the use of data from your personal emails and photos to customize the advertisements you see.

cooked.headline: Starlink still has a 'terms and conditions' speed limit for war zones
cooked.summary: Zelenskyy confirmed that Starlink's performance caps are still active, proving that even satellite internet has a strict 'fair use' policy for international conflicts. It turns out you can't just bypass global geopolitics with a firmware update.
cooked.plain_english: The Ukrainian government stated that Starlink services continue to be subject to speed and usage restrictions.

cooked.headline: Google is being sued for taking pictures of the things it built maps to see.
cooked.summary: German courts have decided that Google's aerial imagery is essentially spying, which is a bold stance for a country that relies on the exact same maps to find their way to lunch. It turns out that being the world's most detailed stalker is only acceptable until the legal team starts looking at the fine print.
cooked.plain_english: A German court has ruled that Google's collection of high-resolution aerial photography constitutes an illegal invasion of privacy.

cooked.headline: Google speedran deforestation to build a data center in Finland.
cooked.summary: Google decided to clear-cut 250,000 trees without a permit, proving that their 'carbon neutral' goals are apparently flexible when there is compute to be deployed. It is the ultimate corporate side quest: save the planet in the README, but delete the forest in production.
cooked.plain_english: Google cut down 250,000 trees in Finland to build a data center without obtaining the necessary environmental permits.

cooked.headline: Indian government sites are still using revoked certs, because security is just a suggestion
cooked.summary: The Indian government is serving revoked certificates like they are expired coupons at a grocery store checkout. It turns out that when you ignore browser warnings, you aren't just living dangerously; you're essentially hosting a public security fire drill.
cooked.plain_english: Several official Indian government websites are using digital security certificates that have been officially cancelled and deemed invalid.
